\chapter{Writing --- Four Lines That Hold Together}
\label{ch:escribir-cuatro-lineas}
\hlchaptermodality{418}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write four connected lines to a named reader about what I did yesterday, using y to add and porque to give a reason, so that a line depends on the one before it.}

Complete ES-W02-cuatro-lineas-ayer: four lines to one named reader, at least one joined with y and at least one with porque, then cover line one and check line two still needs it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ayer]{Four lines to one person — where the second needs the first}

\label{lesson:ES-W02-cuatro-lineas-ayer}



\begin{quote}
The last writing lesson asked for lines that were \textbf{correct}. This one asks for lines that \textbf{hold together}, which is a different thing and a harder one.

Pick one person who will read this. A real one. You will need them in a moment.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
Connected writing is not \textbf{longer} writing. Four short lines can be connected, and one long line can fail to be.

What makes writing connected is that a sentence stops standing on its own — line two is about line one, and a reader who skipped line one would not follow it.

Spanish gives you exactly two words for that at this point, and they do opposite jobs. \textbf{y} adds one thing to another. \textbf{porque} puts one thing \emph{under} another and says it is the reason.

That is the whole difference between a list and a paragraph. A list can be read in any order. A paragraph cannot.

\subsection*{Writing — connected composition}
Write \textbf{four lines} about yesterday, addressed to the person you picked. Greet them, tell them two things you did, and close.

At least one line must use \textbf{y}, and at least one must use \textbf{porque}.

A worked example, from words you already hold:

\begin{quote}
Hola. Ayer fui a la tienda y comí pan. Hablé con mi amiga porque tuve tiempo. Hasta luego.
\end{quote}

Now write your own four. Do not copy the example — it is there to show the \textbf{shape}, and its second and third lines are the only ones doing the work.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Cover your first line and read the second on its own. Does it still make sense without the first?

If it does, you wrote a \textbf{list}. That is not a failure — it is the stage you were at one lesson ago — but go back and make one line depend on another before you stop.

And read it as the person you named would. Writing for a reader you can picture is the part that makes this a real task rather than an exercise, and it is the part the exam will keep asking for at every level above this one.
\end{tcolorbox}
